career-ready-support.title: Job-ready: customer support, BPO and IT helpdesk
career-ready-support.description: Day-to-day scenario and ticket labs for customer support, BPO chat/voice and IT helpdesk L1, with mock interviews, resume bullet banks and 30-60-90-day plans. Independent practice material with simulated tools.

courses.title: Customer support and BPO: your first day on voice and chat
courses.summary: What a customer-support or BPO job really involves: voice and non-voice queues, the metrics (AHT, FCR, CSAT), the call and chat structure, and how to stay calm with a difficult customer.
outcomes: Open, control and close a call or chat using a clear structure
Calculate AHT, FCR, CSAT and service level from raw numbers
Choose words that de-escalate instead of inflame
Handle an angry customer end to end

lessons.title: Lab: Open and control a voice call

scenes.text: Ritu is on day 6 of nesting. A caller says: 'Your internet has been down since morning and nobody cares!'
She wants to apologise for ten seconds, but the call timer is running and the customer is shouting.

steps.title: The call structure
steps.body: Greeting → verify identity → listen and probe → act or explain → confirm → close. Every call follows the same skeleton, so you never freeze.

steps.title: Empathy + ownership
steps.body: Say what you will do, not what you cannot. 'I understand how frustrating this is, I'll check it right now' beats 'It's not my department'.

steps.title: Dead air
steps.body: Never leave silence longer than ~8 seconds. Say 'May I place you on a short hold while I check?' and wait for a yes.

a.text: Caller: 'Internet down since morning! Fix it NOW.' What is your first response?

choices.label: Apologise, empathise, then verify the account
choices.feedback: Good. Short empathy and then move to verification so you can act.

choices.label: Ask him to calm down
choices.feedback: Telling an angry person to calm down usually raises the volume.

choices.label: Transfer immediately to the technical team

b.text: Verified. The system shows an area outage affecting 400 homes, ETA 3 pm. What next?

choices.label: Explain the outage, ETA, offer an SMS update and confirm he is fine with it
Promise it will be fixed in an hour
choices.feedback: Never promise what you cannot control.

c.text: The customer is now angrier. You recover by owning the issue.

choices.label: Acknowledge, apologise again and verify the account
choices.feedback: Recovery works when you re-own the call.

end1.text: The caller says thanks and the call closes within target AHT. CSAT is likely high.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of a standard support call?
options: Greet, verify, listen/probe, resolve, confirm, close
quiz.why: A fixed skeleton keeps you in control.

quiz.q: A customer is shouting. The best first move is to
options: Acknowledge the feeling briefly and take ownership
quiz.why: Acknowledgement lowers heat; ownership gives direction.

quiz.q: Placing a customer on hold requires
options: Asking permission and giving a reason
quiz.why: Always ask, explain, and return within the promised time.

lessons.title: Lab: Chat and email tone sorter

scenes.text: Arjun handles three chats together. Replies that sound robotic or rude drop CSAT quickly.
His team lead sends a sheet of sample replies to classify.

steps.title: Non-voice rules
steps.body: Chat and email lack tone of voice, so words carry everything. Use short sentences, the customer's name, and signal what you are doing ('Checking now, back in 2 minutes').

steps.title: Concurrency
steps.body: Chat agents usually handle 2–3 chats at once. Use saved replies for greetings but personalise the second line.

steps.title: Capital letters and slang
steps.body: ALL CAPS reads as shouting; slang and emojis can look unprofessional unless the brand allows them.

activity.prompt: Sort each reply: professional or needs rewrite

items.text: Hi Meena, I'm checking this now and will update you in 2 minutes.
U need to wait, system is down.
I understand the delay is frustrating. Here is what I can do right now.
THAT IS NOT OUR POLICY.
Thank you for waiting. I've raised a request; your reference is SR-20418.
Not my job, ask billing.

quiz.q: In chat support, long silences are best avoided by

options: A summary of action taken, next step and reference number

quiz.q: Why avoid ALL CAPS in chat?
quiz.why: Tone is carried only by text.

lessons.title: Lab: Support metrics calculator

scenes.text: Team lead Sana shows the numbers: 800 contacts, 640 solved at first contact, 180 survey replies, 153 satisfied.
Sana asks the new joiners to compute the metrics.

steps.title: The four numbers
steps.body: FCR = contacts resolved at first contact ÷ total × 100. CSAT = satisfied (4–5 on a 5-point scale) ÷ survey responses × 100. AHT = talk + hold + after-call work. Service level = % answered within a threshold (for example 80% in 20 seconds).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: AHT: talk 330 s + hold 45 s + wrap-up 75 s = 450 s = 7.5 min. In 6 productive hours (21,600 s) an agent can take 21,600 ÷ 450 = 48 calls.

steps.title: Don't game metrics
steps.body: Rushing a call to lower AHT reduces FCR and CSAT. Quality and speed move together.

activity.prompt: FCR: 640 of 800 contacts were resolved at first contact. What is FCR in %?

quiz.q: CSAT of 153 satisfied out of 180 responses is about

options: Talk time, hold time and after-call work

quiz.q: Rushing calls to cut AHT typically hurts

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – the angry customer, end to end

scenes.text: A customer finds a ₹1,499 charge he did not expect and says he will go to social media.
You have 8 minutes. Use the whole skeleton.

steps.title: Recovery framework
steps.body: LAST: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank. Then document the case so the next agent doesn't repeat the questions.

steps.title: Documentation
steps.body: Good notes say: what the customer reported, what you checked, what you promised, and by when. This protects both customer and you.

steps.title: Compliance
steps.body: Never read out or ask for full card numbers, OTPs or passwords. Follow the verification script.

s.text: Customer: 'You charged me ₹1,499 and I never asked for it. I'm posting this on social media!'

choices.label: Listen fully, apologise for the confusion, verify the account
Explain that the terms say charges can apply

v.text: You find an add-on activated by a promo. The customer did not consent clearly.

choices.label: Offer to reverse it per policy, explain the timeline and send an SMS confirmation
Ask him to write an email

x.text: The customer is furious and demands a supervisor.

choices.label: Apologise, own the issue and re-verify

e.text: Refund request RR-5521 raised, 5–7 working days, customer thanks you. Notes updated.

options: What was checked, promised and when
quiz.why: Notes carry context to the next agent.

courses.title: Escalations and ticket handling for support agents
courses.summary: Raise, update and escalate tickets like a professional: priorities, SLA clocks, the escalation matrix and closure notes that survive an audit.
outcomes: Choose the right priority and category
Write ticket updates that others can act on
Follow an escalation matrix correctly
Close tickets with complete resolution notes

lessons.title: Lab: Ticket – double charge on the bill

scenes.text: Customer Neha sees two identical debits on her broadband bill.
You must raise and resolve the ticket within SLA.

steps.title: Anatomy of a ticket
steps.body: Reporter, category, priority, description, steps taken, SLA clock and status. A good description lets a stranger continue without calling the customer again.

steps.title: Check before escalating
steps.body: Look at the account ledger, payment gateway reference and previous tickets before you pass it on.

steps.title: Duplicates
steps.body: Search for an existing ticket first; duplicate tickets split the history and waste time.

ticket.description: hi i paid my bill on 3rd and the amount came twice in my bank sms. pls refund asap or i will cancel connection

investigate.label: Check payment gateway log
investigate.reveal: Two captures: TXN 88120 and TXN 88121, 41 seconds apart, same invoice INV-7731, both 'success'.

investigate.label: Check invoice status
investigate.reveal: Invoice INV-7731 shows paid once; the second credit sits as unallocated.

investigate.label: Ask customer to restart router
investigate.reveal: No relation to billing.

investigate.label: Check last ticket history
investigate.reveal: No earlier tickets.

options: Duplicate payment capture; second payment unallocated
diagnosis.why: The gateway shows two successful captures for one invoice.

resolution: Verify customer identity
Confirm the duplicate in gateway and ledger
Raise a refund request to finance with both TXN ids
Tell the customer the timeline and reference
Update the ticket and set it to pending refund

closure.model: Customer paid INV-7731 twice (TXN 88120/88121). Duplicate capture confirmed in gateway; second amount unallocated. Raised refund RR-3392 to Finance. Customer informed: credit in 5–7 working days. Ticket pending refund confirmation.

quiz.q: Which detail helps most in a ticket description?
options: Exact transaction IDs and what was checked

quiz.q: Before raising a new ticket you should
A customer was charged twice. The team that normally returns the money is

lessons.title: Lab: Escalation matrix – put the steps in order

scenes.text: A P2 ticket is 70% through its SLA with no fix. Shalini isn't sure whom to inform.
Her team lead says: 'Follow the matrix, in order.'

steps.title: Levels
steps.body: L1 agent → L2 specialist → team lead → manager → vendor or major-incident team. You escalate with facts, not feelings.

steps.title: Functional vs hierarchical
steps.body: Functional escalation moves a ticket to a more skilled team. Hierarchical escalation informs a manager when time or customer impact is high.

steps.title: Don't skip levels
steps.body: Jumping to a manager for a P4 ticket hurts your credibility.

activity.prompt: Put a proper escalation in order
items: Attempt L1 fixes and document them
Hand over to L2 with a full summary
Inform the customer of the new owner and ETA
Follow up before the SLA breaches

options: Moving to a team with more skill
Symptoms, steps tried, evidence, customer impact
When SLA or business impact is at risk

lessons.title: Lab: Ticket – refund stuck in 'processing'

scenes.text: A refund was promised 9 days ago. The customer calls for the third time.
You must find what is blocking it.

steps.title: Follow the trail
steps.body: Ticket → refund request → finance queue → bank. Each hop has an owner and a status; find where it stopped.

steps.title: Typical blockers
steps.body: Wrong bank details, missing approval, batch cut-off, or a transfer rejected by the bank.

steps.title: Tell the truth
steps.body: If it is delayed, say so, say why and give a real next date.

ticket.short: Refund promised 9 days ago, still not received
ticket.description: This is my 3rd call!! Refund RR-3101 was supposed to come in 5-7 days. Nobody tells me anything.

investigate.label: Open refund request RR-3101
investigate.reveal: Status: 'Returned by bank' – beneficiary account number mismatch.

investigate.label: Check customer's plan
investigate.reveal: Plan is active, irrelevant.

investigate.label: Read prior call notes
investigate.reveal: Agent promised 5-7 days; bank details were never re-verified.

investigate.label: Ask customer to wait 3 more days
investigate.reveal: Would breach SLA and leave the issue unsolved.

options: The bank returned it due to a beneficiary mismatch
diagnosis.why: The RR status shows the return reason.

resolution: Apologise and take ownership
Verify and correct bank details with the customer
Ask Finance to re-initiate RR-3101
Give the customer a new realistic date
Add notes and set a follow-up reminder

closure.model: RR-3101 returned by bank (beneficiary mismatch). Verified corrected details with customer, asked Finance to re-initiate; new ETA 3 working days. Follow-up set for day 3.

quiz.q: A refund shows 'Returned by bank'. Most likely action?
options: Correct the account details and re-initiate
Tell the customer to try later
quiz.why: Fix the data, not the story.

quiz.q: If the delay is your side's fault you should
options: Apologise and give a firm new date
So the promise is kept before the customer calls again

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – prioritise a queue of tickets

scenes.text: Six tickets arrive together. Which first?
Priority comes from impact and urgency, not from who shouts loudest.

steps.title: Impact × urgency
steps.body: P1: many users or full outage; P2: a major function broken for a few; P3: single user, workaround exists; P4: question or request.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Payment gateway down for all customers = P1. One customer's invoice typo = P4.

steps.title: Loudest is not highest
steps.body: Customer tone does not change priority; business impact does.

courses.title: IT helpdesk L1: triage and first-line fixes
courses.summary: Work like a real L1 analyst: read vague tickets, ask the right questions, fix the common problems (passwords, printers, VPN) and know exactly when to escalate.
outcomes: Triage tickets by impact and urgency
Ask short, targeted diagnostic questions
Resolve the common L1 issues
Escalate with evidence to L2

lessons.title: Lab: Ticket – locked account before a client meeting

scenes.text: Sales rep Isha cannot log in; client demo at 9:30.
Account lockout is the L1 classic.

steps.title: Identity first
steps.body: Verify the caller using the approved method (employee ID plus manager name or callback). Never reset an account just because someone sounds sure.

steps.title: Why lockouts happen
steps.body: Mistyped passwords, a stale saved password on a phone mail app, or a mapped drive using old credentials.

steps.title: Don't share passwords
steps.body: Set a temporary password via the tool and force a change at next sign-in.

ticket.description: my account is not working, pls fix, demo at 9.30!! tried many times

investigate.label: Check account in directory
investigate.reveal: Status: locked out at 08:31 after 5 bad attempts. Password last changed 31 days ago.

investigate.label: Check last bad-password source
investigate.reveal: Source: ISHA-ANDROID (mail app) – old password stored on phone.

investigate.label: Reimage the laptop
investigate.reveal: Overkill; wastes hours.

investigate.label: Check VPN logs
investigate.reveal: No VPN events; not related.

options: Phone mail app retrying an old password, causing the lockout
diagnosis.why: The bad-password source is the phone.

resolution: Verify identity
Unlock the account
Ask the user to update the saved password on the phone
Test sign-in with the user
Document and close

closure.model: Account locked after 5 bad attempts from a mobile mail app with an old password. Identity verified, account unlocked, phone password updated. User confirmed login working.

quiz.q: The first step before resetting any account is
A repeat lockout after a reset is often caused by
options: A device with an old saved password
Confirm with the user before closing

lessons.title: Lab: Triage sort – L1 fix or escalate?

scenes.text: Rahul has 12 tickets. Some he can fix; others need L2.
He keeps a simple rule: fix known issues, escalate unknown or high-risk.

steps.title: What L1 owns
steps.body: Password reset, printer mapping, mail profile, basic VPN, software from the catalogue, and how-to questions.

steps.title: Knowledge base first
steps.body: Search the KB before escalating; most tickets have a documented fix.

steps.title: Security signals
steps.body: Phishing clicks, ransomware notes or unusual admin activity go to the security team immediately.

items.text: Reset forgotten password
Server room smells of burning
Map shared printer
User clicked a phishing link and entered password
Outlook profile corrupt

lessons.title: Lab: Ticket – shared printer offline for a floor

scenes.text: Fifteen finance staff cannot print; month-end close is today.
SLA is 4 hours; every minute counts.

steps.title: Scope first
steps.body: One user or all users? One printer or many? Scope tells you whether to look at the device, the print server or the network.

steps.title: Common causes
steps.body: Stuck spooler, printer IP changed after a DHCP lease, paper/toner error, or a paused queue on the print server.

steps.title: Ping then queue
steps.body: Ping the printer; if it replies, look at the queue; if not, check cable and IP.

ticket.description: none of us can print since morning. printer shows ready. pls urgent month end

investigate.label: Ping printer 192.168.30.45
investigate.reveal: Request timed out.

investigate.label: Check print server queue
investigate.reveal: Queue healthy; jobs waiting with error 'printer offline'.

investigate.label: Check DHCP lease table
investigate.reveal: Printer MAC now has 192.168.30.77; old IP 192.168.30.45 is assigned to a laptop.

investigate.label: Reinstall drivers on one PC
investigate.reveal: Not related to a floor-wide failure.

options: The printer's IP changed via DHCP; the port still points to the old IP
diagnosis.why: New IP found in the DHCP table.

resolution: Confirm scope: all users, same printer
Find the printer's current IP
Update the port on the print server
Print a test page
Request a DHCP reservation for the printer

closure.model: Printer received new DHCP address 192.168.30.77; server port pointed at old IP. Updated port, test print OK, requested DHCP reservation (CHG-2280) to prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: A DHCP reservation for a printer
If ping to a printer times out, check
options: Power, cable and its IP address

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – VPN won't connect from home

scenes.text: Deepa works from home; the VPN says 'Connection failed'.
She is stressed; there is a deadline today.

steps.title: Layered thinking
steps.body: Check the user's internet, then the VPN client, then credentials/MFA, then the gateway. Work from the nearest layer outward.

steps.title: Ask for the exact message
steps.body: 'Connection failed' differs from 'Authentication failed'. The wording changes the path.

steps.title: Don't disable security
steps.body: Never tell users to turn off the firewall or MFA to 'just try'.

ticket.description: vpn not working from home since yesterday, error says something about certificate

investigate.label: Check user's internet
investigate.reveal: Browsing works fine.

investigate.label: Read VPN client log
investigate.reveal: Error 812: device certificate expired on 24-Nov.

investigate.label: Check VPN gateway status
investigate.reveal: Gateway healthy; other users connected.

investigate.label: Reset user's password
investigate.reveal: Authentication is not the problem.

diagnosis.why: The log shows an expired certificate.

resolution: Confirm internet works
Read the client log for the exact error
Renew the device certificate through the portal
Reconnect and test
Record cause and close

closure.model: VPN failed with error 812 (expired device certificate). Renewed certificate via self-service, reconnected successfully, user confirmed access to internal apps.

lessons.title: Lab: ipconfig – no internet, find the clue

scenes.text: A laptop shows connected but no website opens.
You ask the user to read their IP address.

steps.title: APIPA
steps.body: An address starting 169.254.x.x means the PC could not reach a DHCP server and gave itself an address. No gateway is normally present.

steps.title: What to read
steps.body: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers.

steps.title: Don't guess
steps.body: Run the command and read the actual output. This console is simulated.

lessons.title: Lab: DNS or connectivity? ping and nslookup

scenes.text: Users can ping 10.20.0.10 but 'portal.example.com' will not open.

steps.title: Test in layers
steps.body: Ping an IP (tests connectivity). Ping a name (tests DNS). If the IP works and the name fails, DNS is the suspect.

steps.title: nslookup
steps.body: Shows which server answered and what address the name resolves to.

steps.title: Flush
steps.body: ipconfig /flushdns clears stale cached answers on the PC.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – questions you will actually be asked

scenes.text: Tanvi is nervous about her first BPO interview.
The recruiter says: 'Tell me about yourself, then a time you handled an angry person.'

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Use STAR for stories: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Keep answers around 60–90 seconds.

steps.title: Language
steps.body: BPO rounds often include a voice and grammar screen; speak slowly and clearly, and avoid fillers.

steps.title: Never badmouth
steps.body: Criticising a previous employer or teacher marks you as a risk.

activity.prompt: Practise out loud. Read each model answer and then say your own version.

items.a: Give four lines: current status, one strength, one relevant skill, why this role. 'I'm a commerce graduate, patient with people, comfortable typing at 40 wpm, and I want a career in customer support.'
I enjoy solving problems for people and communicating clearly; support gives quick feedback and a path to team lead, quality or trainer roles.

items.q: How do you handle an angry customer?
items.a: I listen without interrupting, apologise for the experience, verify details, take ownership and give a clear next step with a timeline. I stay calm and don't take it personally.

items.q: Are you comfortable with night shifts?
items.a: Answer honestly. Say yes only if you have considered the schedule and travel.

items.q: What if you don't know the answer?
items.a: I say 'Let me check that for you', search the knowledge base, ask a senior if needed and call back if promised.

items.q: Where do you see yourself in three years?
items.a: Growing into a senior agent or quality analyst, building domain skills and helping new joiners.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – role-play, the refund request

scenes.text: The interviewer plays an annoyed customer who wants a refund outside policy.
They watch tone, structure and honesty.

steps.title: What they score
steps.body: Greeting, empathy, accuracy, control, closing and policy discipline.

steps.title: Say your actions
steps.body: 'I'll check this for you' shows you are active.

steps.title: No false promises
steps.body: Never promise a refund you can't authorise.

a.text: Interviewer: 'I bought this last month. I want my money back NOW.'

choices.label: Empathise, ask for order details, explain policy and options
Acknowledge, offer exchange or store credit, offer to escalate

c.text: You have promised something outside policy.

end.text: You are scored high on empathy, honesty and control.

lessons.title: Lab: Resume bullet bank – strong vs weak

scenes.text: Aman's resume says 'Responsible for customer calls'.
A mentor shows him how to add numbers and outcomes.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Action verb + what + how many or how well + result. 'Resolved 45+ customer queries per day with 92% CSAT.'

steps.title: Fresher bullets
steps.body: 'Ran the college fest helpdesk for 3 days, answering 200+ visitor queries'; 'Completed typing course: 42 wpm at 96% accuracy'.

steps.title: Only true numbers
steps.body: Never invent figures; recruiters may verify.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – your 30-60-90-day plan

scenes.text: Meera joins as a support agent. Her manager asks, 'What will you do in 30, 60 and 90 days?'
She opens her plan.

steps.title: Days 1–30: learn
steps.body: Master product, tools and scripts; shadow calls; complete certification; ask for feedback weekly.

steps.title: Days 31–60: perform
steps.body: Hit AHT and quality targets; handle common issues alone; start a personal FAQ sheet.

steps.title: Days 61–90: contribute
steps.body: Mentor a new joiner, suggest one process fix with data, discuss your growth path (senior agent, QA, trainer, L2).
